Accumulation Rate Curve (ARC) Richness Estimator

Source: R/arc.R
arc.Rd

Estimate total species richness from the rate at which new species appear along a random reordering of the observations (Shestopaloff 2025). The rate curve is extrapolated with three decay curves whose tails give the number of species not yet seen, combined with bounded weights.

Usage

arc(
  x,
  data = c("abundance", "incidence"),
  K = 20L,
  adjust = FALSE,
  n_boot = 2000L,
  parallel = TRUE,
  n_cores = NULL
)

Arguments

x

A site-by-species matrix. For data = "abundance" the columns are pooled into species abundances; for data = "incidence" the matrix is binarized and each species counts the sites it occupies.

data

Character. "abundance" (default) treats every individual as one observation; "incidence" treats every species-site occurrence as one.

K

Integer. Species seen more than K times are left out of the rate curve. Default 20.

adjust

Logical. Apply the smoothing adjustment of Eq. 11 with a log-linear fit to the frequency counts? Default FALSE. See Details.

n_boot

Integer. Parametric bootstrap draws for the interval. Default 2000. 0 returns the point estimate only.

parallel

Logical. Use parallel processing? Default TRUE.

n_cores

Integer. Number of cores.

Value

An object of class spacc_estimate with estimator = "ARC". Its details hold undetected (undetected species from each curve) and weights (their weights), both averaged over the curve portions, K, data, penalty (the selected Poisson-mixture penalty) and boot (the bootstrap estimates).

Details

Let \(y_k\) be the number of species observed \(k\) times and \(N\) the number of observations of the species with \(k \le K\). Drawing the observations in random order, the expected number of these species seen after \(n\) draws is $$S(n) = \sum_{k=1}^{K} y_k \left[1 - (1 - n/N)^k\right],$$ and the accumulation rate is \(s_n = S(n) - S(n-1)\), evaluated at up to 1000 points. Three curves are fitted to the tail of \(s_n\) by least squares with weights proportional to the squared point index: the log-normal \(1 - \Phi((\log n - \mu)/\sigma)\), the log-logistic \(1/(1 + \alpha n^\gamma)\) and the Weibull \(\exp(-\lambda n^\gamma)\), the last on the log scale. Each curve's integral from \(N\) to infinity is its number of undetected species; the log-logistic integral is finite only for \(\gamma > 1\).

The estimate combines the three with weights fitted by the squared misfit to \(s_n\) plus a penalty on the product of the log-logistic and Weibull weights (Eq. 8), each bounded by caps built from the three estimates and the observed richness (Eq. 7). The undetected species are averaged over fits to the last 100, 95, ..., 70 percent of the curve.

The penalty is there to make the fit prefer either the log-logistic or the Weibull, and gives the loss one local minimum for each. The weights are the end point of the projected gradient flow of the loss started at zero weights, which arc() solves in closed form face by face of the box of admissible weights. This is the minimum the author's reference code reaches (L-BFGS within an augmented Lagrangian, started at zero). In Poisson-Gamma samples of intermediate sparsity it is the log-logistic one, with median bias between -1 and +4 percent; the global minimum of the loss is the Weibull one there, with median bias between -9 and -17 percent (vignette("richness-estimation")).

With adjust = TRUE the counts \(y_1, \dots, y_{k_1}\) (the first run of positive counts) are mixed half and half with a log-linear fit \(\log y_k = b_0 + b_1 k\), and fully replaced by it; the adjusted estimate is \(2 S_{0.5} - S_1\). The adjustment assumes the ratios \((k+1) y_{k+1} / y_k\) are linear in \(k\).

The interval comes from a parametric bootstrap of the counts. Their covariance is that of a mixture of 30 Poisson distributions whose weights are fitted to \((y_1, \dots, y_K, y_{K+})\) by penalised least squares (Eq. 12-15). The penalty is chosen by resampling species: 1500 resamples are ordered by their distance to the left-out species and split into deciles, and the first decile whose out-of-sample error is smallest at a non-zero penalty sets it. n_boot count vectors are drawn from a normal distribution with that covariance, rounded to non-negative integers and re-estimated; the interval is their 2.5 and 97.5 percent quantiles and the standard error their standard deviation. In Poisson-Gamma simulations the 95 percent interval covered the truth in 93 to 96 percent of samples for sparse data and about 89 percent for dense data, where the point estimate is biased upwards (vignette("richness-estimation")).

With data = "incidence" the observations are species-site occurrences and \(y_k\) becomes \(Q_k\), the number of species found at \(k\) sites, the substitution that turns Chao1 into Chao2.

References

Shestopaloff, K. (2025). An accumulation rate curve estimator for total species. Environmental and Ecological Statistics, 32, 311-345. doi:10.1007/s10651-025-00644-y

See also

chao1(), chao2(), ace()

Examples

set.seed(1)
species <- matrix(rpois(40 * 300, rgamma(300, 0.4, 2)), nrow = 40, byrow = TRUE)
arc(species, n_boot = 0)
# \donttest{
arc(species, n_boot = 200)
# }
